proof_text:
Let $(a_n)$ be a bounded real sequence. Thus there exists a closed
bounded interval $I_0 = [a, b]$ containing every term: $a_n \in I_0$
for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

We construct a nested sequence of closed intervals
$I_0 \supset I_1 \supset I_2 \supset \cdots$ via the bisection method:
1. Bisect $I_0 = [a, b]$ at its midpoint $m = (a + b)/2$ into two
   subintervals $[a, m]$ and $[m, b]$. At least one subinterval
   contains $a_n$ for infinitely many indices $n$. Choose such a
   subinterval and denote it $I_1 = [a_1, b_1]$. Its length is
   $(b - a)/2$.
2. Continuing inductively, having constructed $I_k$ containing
   infinitely many terms of the sequence, bisect $I_k$ and select a
   half $I_{k+1}$ containing infinitely many terms. The length of
   $I_k$ is $|I_k| = (b - a)/2^k$.

Now choose a subsequence $(a_{n_k})$: choose $n_1$ such that
$a_{n_1} \in I_1$. Having chosen $n_1 < n_2 < \dots < n_k$ with
$a_{n_k} \in I_k$, since $I_{k+1}$ contains infinitely many terms of
the sequence, we can choose $n_{k+1} > n_k$ such that
$a_{n_{k+1}} \in I_{k+1}$.

By the Nested Interval Theorem, $\bigcap_{k=1}^\infty I_k = \{L\}$ for
a unique real number $L$. Since both $a_{n_k}$ and $L$ belong to
$I_k$, we have: $$ |a_{n_k} - L| \leq |I_k| = \frac{b - a}{2^k}. $$
Since $\lim_{k \to \infty} (b - a)/2^k = 0$, it follows that
$a_{n_k} \to L$ as $k \to \infty$. Thus every bounded real sequence
possesses a convergent subsequence.

Theorem:
given: S ::= a(n_) is \(bounded)::real.sequence
then:
. exists:
  . T ::= b(k_) is \subsequence:of{S}
  . L is \real
  suchThat: \converges.to{L}:for{T}
